 With Democrats in charge of Texas, what's next for UT Austin? 
 KUT 90.5 | 
 By
 Neena Satija 
 Published November 5, 2026 at 5:00 AM CST
 Facebook 
 Twitter 
 LinkedIn 
 Email 
 Gabriel C. Pérez 
 / 
 KUT News Texas controls public universities in two crucial ways: The governor appoints everyone on their oversight boards, and the Legislature controls their budgets and the policies they operate under. 
 Under Texas Republicans’ leadership, UT Austin has been undergoing a sea change. In just the last two years, the school installed new top leadership, slashed numerous majors , launched an overhaul of its core curriculum , and intervened in the governance of KUT Public Media – Austin’s NPR station that the university has housed for decades.
 What could happen now that Democrats, who have harshly criticized many of those changes, are about to take charge?
 The state controls Texas’ public universities in two crucial ways. The governor appoints everyone on their oversight boards, including nine voting members of the Board of Regents for the University of Texas System, which includes UT Austin and a dozen other public institutions. And, the Texas Legislature controls their budgets and the policies they operate under.
 Both levers of control could transform following the midterm elections, though not immediately.
 UT Austin did not respond to a request for comment.
 KUT and KUTX are editorially independent from UT . They are funded by community and business donations, rather than state taxpayer dollars or student tuition.
 Oversight board will take time to change  
 Texas Gov. Greg Abbott has packed the UT System Board of Regents , who serve six-year staggered terms, with conservative donors and allies.
 Gina Hinojosa, who defeated Abbott to become the state’s first Democratic governor in more than three decades, will now be in charge of filling those seats. But six of the nine regents are not up for reappointment until 2029 or later, unless they choose to leave sooner. Hinojosa does not have the power to fire them outright. The Texas Senate, which still has a Republican majority, must also confirm Hinojosa's picks — if she makes them while the Legislature is in session. 
 UT’s former top spokesman Gary Susswein said that could limit Hinojosa’s ability to make sweeping changes right away.
 Susswein, who now runs a strategic communications firm in Austin, pointed out that former Texas Gov. Rick Perry repeatedly clashed with the regents he had chosen. He wanted them to fire then UT President Bill Powers, and for years, they resisted.
 “Regents don’t always follow the governor’s lead on campus leadership,” Susswein said.
 Three of the regents’ terms will expire next February. One of them is Board Chair Kevin Eltife, a former Republican state senator who has been heavily involved in the running of UT Austin and who played a key role in bringing a new conservative think tank there.
 Hinojosa’s campaign did not immediately respond to a request for comment on the matter, but there’s a good chance she will try replace at least some of the regents as soon as she is able. Like many Texas Democrats, she has previously accused UT of stifling free speech to placate conservative leaders.
 “I will appoint members of the boards of regents who are respectful of academic freedom,” Hinojosa told the student newspaper for the University of Texas at Tyler earlier this year.
 Recent legislation targeting higher education now in flux  
 Two laws passed in recent years by Texas’ Republican-led Legislature have been reshaping higher education across the state. Senate Bill 17 banned “diversity, equity, and inclusion” offices and programs at public universities. Senate Bill 37 gave the governor-appointed regents far more power over how the universities are run, and it also created a new state office that could investigate the colleges for violating the new laws.
 UT Austin leaders cited those laws when deciding to eliminate certain majors, lay off dozens of staff , and limit the influence of university faculty in decision-making.
 The laws will still be on the books when winners of the midterms take office next year. It’s unclear if that could change during the upcoming legislative session, given that Republicans still have control of the Texas State Senate. But Susswein noted that Texas’ top elected officials and the regents play a big role in how they’re implemented.
 “The real test is how they’re carried out with an incoming governor, lieutenant governor and attorney general who all voted against them as legislators,” Susswein said. He was referring to Hinojosa, Vikki Goodwin, and Nathan Johnson, respectively. Before they were all elected to statewide office this week, they were Democrats in the Legislature who opposed the Republican-led changes to higher education policy.
 Republican State Sen. Paul Bettencourt, who is currently the chair of the state senate’s higher education committee, said he thought UT Austin had done “the best job” carrying out the new laws and that they had not had a negative impact.
 He added that Davis had recently told him the university had gotten 1,000 applicants for one open job.
 “If the system isn’t broke, why are we fixing it?” he said.
 What does this mean for KUT? 
 Ever since UT Austin fired KUT Public Media general manager Debbie Hiott earlier this year, observers in political, media and higher education circles have wondered whether the university’s conservative leadership would target the radio station in other ways.
 The university has said it fired Hiott due to her mismanagement of the inaugural KUT Festival, though KUT News has reported on a trove of internal records disputing that account. Hiott, in turn, has argued that the station should separate from the university in order to avoid further political interference.
 Hiott said she feels the same way following the midterm elections.
 “To me, it doesn’t matter who is in the Legislature and it doesn’t matter who is in the executive branch of the state government when it comes to that issue,” Hiott said. "Ultimately, I just don’t think that KUT should be at risk of the whims of any political party.”
 Still, she said, she expects the newly elected statewide leaders to broadly support public media across the state in contrast to their Republican counterparts. “That could be beneficial to the stations,” she said, referencing other university-licensed public radio stations.
 ‘This is just a tremendous opportunity’ 
 The Democratic sweep in Texas came as such a surprise, the newly elected leaders may not have yet considered exactly what their plans will be for UT Austin or other public institutions.
 “The balance of power will take a while to shift,” said Art Markman, a former UT professor and senior vice provost who said he was dismissed from his post over “ideological differences” last year. “On the other hand, it’s also clear that the people of Texas spoke with a loud voice.”
 Markman said he clashed with recent UT leadership because he believed they were making “heavy handed” changes to academics “without an attempt to bring people along.” He said he was optimistic that the new state leaders would take a different approach, adding that he believes higher education has long been in need of transformation — just not in the manner that Texas Republicans have pushed for.
 “Public trust does need to be restored in public education,” Markman, who now lives in California, said. “This is just a tremendous opportunity for one of the great universities in the world.”
 Editor’s note: KUT journalists are University of Texas employees. Editorial decisions are made independently by the KUT newsroom. University leaders do not review or approve KUT’s news coverage. 
 Disclosure: Markman is co-host of the podcast Two Guys on Your Head which airs on KUT News. He is not an employee of the news organization. 
 Support for KUT's reporting on education news comes from  UT's Human Dimensions of Organizations . Sponsors do not influence KUT's editorial decisions.
